newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan stocks slow at start of week.
newsitem.headline: Jordan stocks slow at start of week.

text.p: Jordanian stocks were slow at the start of weekly trade amid fears of a worsening of ties with Baghdad following allegations of Iraqi involvement in recent unrest, dealers said on Saturday.
The official Amman Financial Market 60-share index was hardly changed from Wednesday's 139.54 points -- it fell a slight 0.01 percent -- and remained below the key psychological barrier of 140.

"The market is very weak today with no buying orders and while the market was assured over return of calm, on one side, the fear of a deterioration in ties with Iraqi cast a negative sentiment on the overall market," said one broker.
Many of Jordan's industrial firms partly rely on the Iraqi market.
The stock market, already suffering from a lack of cash liquidity and limited institutional support, has fallen by just under one percent since two days of rioting last week.
The riots, the worst since 1989 unrest, were fuelled by the government's decision to almost double bread prices in line with IMF-agreed economic reforms.
A total of 172,229 shares changed hands in a low 431,039 dinar turnover, with no demand from foreign investors.
The market first broke the 140-point barrier at the end of June and has since slid to levels not reached since 1993. But it began a gradual pick-up in trade at the start of last week.

Traders said the troubles had increased uncertainty over the country's long-term economic outlook, but the government's tough reaction so far showed its determination to push on with radical IMF-backed economic reforms.
The Pearl Investable Index -- an independent index of the 45 best-performing shares from the official market -- dropped 0.29 percent to 79.96 points. It was 16.28 percent down on last year.
Along with a lack of institutional support, the market has suffered since the start of the year from a liquidity crunch blamed on high interest rates as the state seeks to protect the dinar.
Large investors and institutions have avoided the market, with the official index falling 12-13 percent this year and with most of the business dominated by floor traders.

Banks dominated in a 200,287 dinar turnover and an index rise of 0.17 percent, industrials had a 161,428 dinar turnover and an index drop of 0.21 percent while services had a 61,970 dinar turnover and an index drop of 0.54 percent.
A total of 208,890 shares worth 80,652 dinars changed hands in weak trade in the parallel market.
